newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS says dlr could be over- and undervalue.
newsitem.headline: BIS says dlr could be over- and undervalue.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said that the U.S. dollar could be considered overvalued or undervalued, depending on the measure used to judge its level against foreign currencies.
BIS noted in its 67th annual report that a stronger dollar has helped to balance out world demand, especially favouring countries such as those in Europe with weak growth.
The stronger dollar also helped to reduce risk of overheating in the U.S. economy by making imports less expensive in dollar terms.
"However, from a longer-term perspective, the question arises as to whether the current level of the dollar is consistent with fundamentals," BIS said.
"Judged against its purchasing power the dollar remains undervalued: travellers still find goods and services cheaper in the U.S. than in Europe or Japan," BIS said.

But, based on estimates at which the dollar would achieve a balance between inflows and outflows based on trade and capital flows, which would leave external debt to output stable, the dollar could be overvalued, BIS said. Even purchasing power parity if it is adjusted for productivity showed the dollar overvalued.
"Necessarily problematic estimates suggest that at market rates in May 1997 the dollar is somewhat overvalued against the mark and rather more so against the yen," BIS said.
Its study was published when the dollar was at 1.70 marks and 123 yen earlier in May.

In a table, BIS said that the dollar's purchasing power parity based on a study by the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) last year was estimated at 2.05 marks and 172 yen. Based on a 1992 study produced by Penn World Tables, the levels were 2.12 marks or 188 yen.
But a Goldman Sachs estimate of purchasing power parity adjusted for productivity placed the dollar at 1.51 marks and 112 yen.

BIS also said "the picture looks different" based on fundamental equilibrium exchange rates, defined by BIS as "effective exchange rates compatible with current account imbalances that leave the ratio of external debt to output stable."

A study by the Institute for International Economics produced fundamental equilibrium exchange rates of 1.45 to 1.50 marks and 100 yen. A similar study by Swiss Bank Corp produced levels of 1.42 marks and 94 yen.

The BIS pointed out that the dollar had risen 20 percent against the mark, and 52 percent against the yen by February 8 when Group of Seven finance ministers met in Berlin, from its trough seen in the spring of 1995.
At that meeting the G7 said it was satisfied with the dollar's recovery, and said that "major misalignments in exchange markets" had been corrected.
